question: Does the 2019 Paco and Vitas Nile-tilapia biomonitoring study document fish collected from either estero, or laboratory fish exposed to water collected there?

method.summary: Reviewed the complete publisher-hosted 2019 article PDF, focusing on its abstract and printed pages 687-688 Materials and Methods. Cross-checked the article citation and abstract against the official De La Salle University (DLSU) faculty-research record and a closely matching 2018 DLSU bachelor's-thesis catalog record.
accessNotes: The publisher PDF identifies the article as an Open Access original research paper and exposes its full text. The DLSU faculty-research record displays a 2019 all-rights-reserved notice; no item-specific open reuse license was verified.

The DLSU thesis catalog provides its title, authors, abstract, accession number, and physical description but states that the document is currently unavailable. The thesis methods and any underlying dataset were not inspected.
No local copies of the article, thesis, figures, tables, or datasets were retained.
method.reuseFinding: Public access to the publisher PDF is not treated as permission to republish article text, tables, images, or underlying data. This review records concise attributed methods and provenance only.

sourceFindings.scope: Alam et al. (2019) identify Estero de Paco and Estero de Vitas as the two study-water sources. The Materials and Methods section says water samples were collected along their banks. It separately says juvenile Nile tilapia (Oreochromis niloticus), 4-5 inches long, were procured from Cartimar pet market in Manila; five fish were placed in laboratory aquaria with filtered and aerated tap water and acclimatized for 24 hours before exposure to the estero-water treatments.
sourceFindings.limits: The fish were market-procured laboratory subjects, not fish captured from Estero de Paco or Estero de Vitas. The design tests biological responses to collected water; it does not survey fish occurrence, catches, abundance, habitat use, or species-by-site field presence in either waterway. The sampled water describes the study's historical collection, not current conditions.
sourceFindings.attribution: Classify the source as laboratory biomonitoring and estero-water exposure only. Do not create an O. niloticus occurrence or checklist row for Paco or Vitas from this article.

sourceFindings.scope: The DLSU catalog records a 2018 bachelor's thesis with a closely matching title, overlapping student authors, adviser Zeba F. Alam, and an abstract describing Nile tilapia exposed to water samples from Estero de Paco and Estero de Vitas. It lists accession CDTU017631, one computer disc, and states that the document is not available in the repository.
sourceFindings.limits: The thesis full text and methods were unavailable. The metadata does not explicitly confirm whether the thesis and 2019 article share exactly the same dataset or sample set.
sourceFindings.attribution: Treat the thesis and article as likely related bibliographic records, not as two independent field surveys. Retain the relationship as unconfirmed and occurrence-ineligible.

relationshipAssessment.2018ThesisAnd2019Article: Likely related study lineage: the titles and abstracts are closely aligned, three student authors overlap, and the article's corresponding author is listed as the thesis adviser. The available catalog metadata does not explicitly confirm a thesis-to-article publication relationship or dataset identity.
relationshipAssessment.decision: Do not count the two records as independent surveys or fish-occurrence sources. The 2019 full-text methods alone establish that the experimental tilapia were purchased for laboratory exposure rather than captured from the named waterways.

scopeAndReuseDecision.decision: Research-only laboratory biomonitoring source; exclude from wild-occurrence and field-checklist evidence.

nonClaims: This study does not establish that Nile tilapia were naturally present in Estero de Paco or Estero de Vitas at the time of the study.
Market procurement in Manila is not a capture-locality record for the Cartimar fish and does not establish their geographic origin.
The measured responses to historical water samples are not current water-quality, contact-safety, harvest, or food-safety advice.
No abundance, catchability, fishing access, legal harvest, season, diet, or current-presence claim is made.
No fish photo, figure, table, station geometry, or raw dataset is admitted for reuse.
nextActions: Use a field-capture, voucher, or site-resolved ichthyofaunal source for any Paco or Vitas fish-presence claim.
Do not pursue the unavailable thesis as an occurrence lead unless DLSU or the authors identify a distinct field-survey dataset with collection provenance.
